title: 未来十年选什么专业?给准大学生的就业证据体检(深入版) — BigCat Deep Research

questions.question: 一份志愿指南写着「某职业每年有 30 万岗位缺口」。按美国劳工统计局（BLS）occupational openings 的定义，这个数字该怎么读？
options: 主要是退休腾出的位置，虽不代表扩张，但对新人而言是确定的入职机会
是该职业此刻未被填补的空缺存量，可以和招聘网站上的空缺数直接对照着看
是十年净增岗位摊到每年的数字，反映了这个职业需求扩张的真实速度
主要是在职者离开后要补的流量，其中过半是转行，该职业甚至可能净萎缩
questions.explanation: 全职业年均 openings 里 97.2% 来自分离，只有 2.8% 来自净增长，而分离的 55.5% 是转去别的职业；前 15 名里有 6 个十年净就业在萎缩。最诱人的「退休腾位」错在把替补当机会：多数分离并不是退休。
questions.question_en: A college-application guide says "this occupation has a shortfall of 300,000 jobs every year." Under the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) definition of occupational openings, how should you read this number?
options_en: Mostly positions vacated by retirement: not a sign of expansion, but a guaranteed entry point for newcomers
The stock of vacancies unfilled in the occupation right now, directly comparable with job-board vacancy counts
Ten-year net job growth spread across the years, reflecting the true pace at which demand is expanding
Mostly a flow replacing people who leave, over half changing fields; the occupation may even be shrinking on net
questions.explanation_en: Across all occupations, 97.2% of average annual openings come from separations and only 2.8% from net growth, and 55.5% of separations are moves into other occupations; 6 of the top 15 occupations are shrinking in net employment over the decade. The most tempting option, "retirements freeing up slots," goes wrong by treating replacement as opportunity: most separations aren't retirements.

questions.question: BLS 公布的十年预测自评，对「照着增长榜选专业」意味着什么？
options: 细分职业因为数据更具体所以比大类更准，错误主要来自宏观总量的估计偏差
粗分层面确有信息，细分职业上只略好于「什么都不变」，而选专业恰在细分层面
预测整体可靠，主要失误集中在 AI 这类技术冲击，排除这些职业后榜单仍可用
它连职业增减方向都判断不准，和瞎猜差不多，因此任何层面都不值得参考
questions.explanation: 这条「聚合层级梯度」是越粗越可信、越细越不可信：判断某职业是否快于整体只有 57%，基线 50%。但也不能写成瞎猜，判断增减方向有 78%，最快五分位命中率约是随机的 2.4 倍，所以结论是粗信号，而不是废纸。
questions.question_en: What do the BLS's own published evaluations of its ten-year projections imply for "choosing a major off the growth rankings"?
options_en: Detailed occupations beat broad groups because the data are more specific; errors come mainly from misjudging macro totals
Coarse levels do carry information, but detailed occupations barely beat "nothing changes," and majors are chosen at the detailed level
The projections are reliable overall, with misses concentrated in tech shocks like AI; exclude those occupations and the rankings still work
They can't even get an occupation's direction of growth or decline right, no better than guessing, so they're worthless at any level
questions.explanation_en: This "aggregation-level gradient" says the coarser the level, the more credible, and the finer, the less credible: judging whether an occupation grows faster than average is right only 57% of the time, against a 50% baseline. But you can't call it blind guessing either: the direction of growth or decline is right 78% of the time, and the fastest quintile's hit rate is about 2.4 times random, so the conclusion is a coarse signal, not waste paper.

questions.question: 分专业失业率数据里，计算机科学（CS）和计算机工程（CE）连续两年偏高，艺术史等专业则一年内大幅跳变。如何读才不犯双标？
options: 艺术史样本小属于噪声，CS/CE 样本大，所以两年高位已经是可靠的结构性信号
CS/CE 年际变动远小于中位专业，说明读数精确，可以据此排出专业间的高低
用同一把噪声尺子：单年区间很宽，CS/CE 两次高读数也还称不上稳定趋势
这些数字都由官方发布，跨版本波动反映的是真实需求变化，应当按字面解读
questions.explanation: 用噪声解释艺术史翻车，就得用同样的标准看 CS/CE：计算机工程的 95% 区间是 4%–11%，连续两次落在同一区间内，「复现」并不提供额外信息。最诱人的错项把「变动小」当成「精确」，但数据发布方根本没有公布专业级样本量。
questions.question_en: In unemployment data by major, computer science (CS) and computer engineering (CE) read high two years running, while majors such as art history jump sharply within a single year. How do you read this without applying a double standard?
options_en: Art history's small sample makes it noise; CS/CE have large samples, so two high years are already a reliable structural signal
CS/CE vary far less year to year than the median major, which shows the readings are precise and can be used to rank majors
Apply the same noise yardstick: single-year intervals are wide, and two high CS/CE readings don't yet amount to a stable trend
These figures are all officially published, so swings between releases reflect real shifts in demand and should be taken at face value
questions.explanation_en: If you invoke noise to explain art history's blowup, you have to hold CS/CE to the same standard: computer engineering's 95% interval is 4% to 11%, and two consecutive readings fall inside the same interval, so the "replication" adds no information. The most tempting wrong option treats "low variation" as "precision," but the data publisher never released sample sizes at the major level.
